items.title: Why architecture exists

verification.expected_output: Learner can demonstrate the concept and explain it.

beginner_mistakes: Jumping straight to microservices — every new Go project starts with a gRPC service in its own repo, separate deployment, and a Kubernetes manifest. The overhead of service boundaries (network calls, serialization, deployment coordination, observability) overwhelms the team before they have product-market fit. Start with a modular monolith; extract services only when there is a proven scalability or team-boundary need.

Using architecture astronaut patterns — implementing hexagonal architecture with 7 layers of interfaces before writing a single business function. The abstractions solve problems that do not exist yet and make the code impossible to navigate. Architecture should be refactored toward, not predicted upfront.

Letting accidental architecture become permanent — the directory structure chosen in week 1 (pkg/, internal/, cmd/) becomes the team's mental model. When the service needs to split, the team is reluctant to restructure because 'that's how we've always done it.' Architecture must be treated as malleable: the right structure for 1K LOC is wrong for 100K LOC.
execution_timeline: Team starts a new Go service: one repo, one main.go, flat package structure
→ 1K LOC: everything is in main.go, easy to navigate, no package boundaries needed
→ 5K LOC: files are split by layer — handlers.go, service.go, store.go — still navigable
→ 20K LOC: handlers.go is 3000 lines, service.go has implicit dependencies, tests take 30s to compile
→ 50K LOC: circular import errors appear because domain types are mixed with storage types
→ Team realizes the architecture is fighting them: every new feature requires changing 5 files in 3 packages
→ Team does architecture refactor: extracts domain package, defines explicit interfaces at package boundaries, uses dependency injection
→ 100K LOC: architecture supports the team — new features add 2-3 files, tests compile in 5s, each package has a clear responsibility
→ Business grows: team splits into two squads, extracts one domain into a separate service
→ Architecture evolves again: service boundary is the package boundary that was already defined in the monolith
failure_modes: Over-engineering at the start — the team spends 3 weeks setting up the 'perfect' architecture (DDD aggregates, CQRS, event sourcing, 5 layers of interfaces) before writing any business logic. By week 4, they have no working product and the architecture assumptions are wrong. Fix: start with the simplest structure that could work; refactor when the structure fights you.

No architecture at all — the team adds files to main.go for 6 months. By month 7, the main package has 50 files with no internal boundaries. Any change breaks 3 unrelated features. Developers are afraid to touch code. Fix: pay down architecture debt incrementally — extract one package per sprint until the structure is navigable.

Architecture by fiat — a senior engineer designs the architecture in isolation and mandates it via a document. The team follows it mechanically but does not understand the tradeoffs. When a new requirement does not fit the architecture, they add hacks instead of evolving it. Fix: architecture decisions must be documented with alternatives considered and tradeoffs explained (ADR format).
hidden_magic_checks: Learner must explain why a flat package structure works at 1K LOC but fails at 100K LOC — the cost of navigating and understanding 100 files in a single namespace grows super-linearly with the number of files.
Learner must identify which of two given directory structures is better for a given scenario (e.g., a billing service vs. a real-time chat service) and explain the tradeoff.
Learner must take a given 5-package Go project with circular import errors and restructure it to eliminate the cycles using interface extraction or package regrouping.
zero_magic.how_go_uses_it: Go architected projects use a package structure that mirrors the domain, not the layers. The convention is: cmd/ (entry points), internal/ (private packages), pkg/ (shared library code). Within internal/, structure by domain boundary (e.g., internal/user/, internal/billing/, internal/orders/) rather than by layer (internal/handlers/, internal/services/, internal/repos/). Each domain package owns its types, business logic, and storage interface. Cross-domain communication uses explicit interfaces defined in the consuming package. The standard library's net/http, database/sql, and encoding/json are the architecture primitives — no framework is required.
zero_magic.mental_model: Architecture is not a blueprint drawn before construction. It is the set of decisions that are expensive to change. A good architecture makes the common case easy and the rare case possible. The right architecture for a startup's 3-person MVP is a single main.go file. The right architecture for a 50-engineer org is domain-aligned packages with explicit interfaces. Architecture evolves with the team size, codebase size, and business complexity. The skill is knowing WHEN to add structure, not knowing how to draw the perfect diagram.
performance_implications: Package boundary crossings in Go incur zero runtime cost — calling a function in another package is the same cost as calling one in the same package. The cost is in cognitive load: the developer must understand both packages and the contract between them.

Interface dispatch costs one pointer indirection (~1ns). This is negligible for business logic but matters in hot loops (e.g., calling a storage interface for every row in a 1M-row batch). Prefer concrete types for performance-critical paths.

Dependency injection at startup (constructing all dependencies in main.go and passing them to NewXxx constructors) adds ~10ms per 100 dependencies. This is acceptable for production but can slow test suites — use lazy initialization or build tags for test-specific wiring.
zero_magic.problem_solved: New Go developers start every project with either no structure (everything in main.go) or over-engineering (5 layers of abstraction for a CRUD service). Both fail at scale. This lesson teaches the third path: start simple, evolve the architecture as the codebase grows, and know the signs that it is time to add structure. The learner practices recognizing these signs and making incremental architecture improvements.
zero_magic.proof_of_understanding: The learner is given a Go project at 3 stages of growth (1K LOC flat, 20K LOC with implicit dependencies, 100K LOC with circular imports). For each stage, they must: (1) identify 3 architecture smells, (2) propose a refactoring plan that can be done incrementally (not a rewrite), and (3) explain the tradeoff (what is easier after the refactor, what is harder).
zero_magic.real_world_usage: Go projects that neglect architecture become unmaintainable at ~50K LOC (the 'Go monolith wall'). Projects like Kubernetes (2M+ LOC Go), Docker, and CockroachDB all went through major architecture refactors as they grew. The pattern is consistent: start with a flat structure, extract domain packages when circular imports appear, extract services when team boundaries form. Architecture in production Go is a continuous evolution, not a one-time design.
step_by_step_execution: Start with one main.go file — at <1K LOC, flat structure is the fastest to navigate
When files exceed 1000 lines each: split by layer (handlers.go, service.go, store.go) — at 5K LOC, layer-based structure reduces file navigation time
When circular imports appear: extract a shared domain package with only types and interfaces — at 20K LOC, domain types must be independent of implementation
When test compilation exceeds 10s: organize packages so tests only depend on their own package — isolate test dependencies per package
When two teams work on the same repo: extract domain boundaries into separate internal packages with explicit API contracts — team A owns internal/billing, team B owns internal/orders
When a team outgrows the monorepo: extract one domain package into a separate service — the existing package boundary becomes the service boundary
Document each architecture decision as an ADR (Architecture Decision Record) — why this structure was chosen, what alternatives were considered, and when to revisit
zero_magic.under_the_hood: Go's package system is the architecture primitive. A package is a unit of compilation, import, and name visibility. Exported names (capitalized) form the package API. Unexported names are internal. This visibility boundary is the cheapest and most effective architecture tool — it forces a clear API surface. Imports create a directed acyclic graph of dependencies. If package A depends on package B, and B depends on A, the Go compiler rejects it. This constraint prevents the worst kind of coupling (circular) at compile time. The go tool's cycle detection runs on every build, making circular imports a compile-time error rather than a runtime surprise.
zero_magic.why_it_exists: Architecture exists because code naturally decays into a Big Ball of Mud without intentional structure. Every file added to main.go increases the cost of every future change. Without architecture, the change cost grows O(n²) with codebase size. With architecture (packages with clear boundaries and explicit dependencies), the change cost grows O(n) — each change affects only one package. Architecture is the difference between a codebase that slows down forever and one that can scale to millions of lines.

items.title: Package boundaries

verification.expected_output: Learner can demonstrate the concept and explain it.

beginner_mistakes: Putting every type in one package — a single models/ or types/ package with 200 exported types has no internal cohesion. Every file imports models, creating coupling across the entire codebase. Any change to any type requires recompiling every dependent package.

Making packages too small — a package with one 5-line type and one 3-line function adds import overhead without any benefit. The cost of understanding a package boundary (what is exported, what is internal, what does the package name mean) must be justified by the cohesion within the package.

Circular imports between related packages — users.go imports orders.go and orders.go imports users.go. The Go compiler rejects this, forcing the developer to either merge the packages or extract shared types into a third package. The circular import is a signal that the boundary is wrong.
execution_timeline: Team creates a flat package: everything in package main with 30 files
→ File count grows: main package has 50 files, 15 exported types, no internal structure
→ Developer needs to add a feature: searches 50 files to find where user creation logic lives → 10 minutes of navigation
→ Team extracts internal/user/ package: User type, CreateUser function, validation logic in one place
→ internal/user/ package has 5 exported symbols and 12 unexported helpers → clear API surface
→ internal/user/ is imported by internal/http/ and internal/billing/ → dependency graph is visible in import statements
→ Circular import hits: internal/order/ needs User type from internal/user/, internal/user/ needs Order type for a method → compiler rejects it
→ Team extracts shared types to internal/user/types/ and internal/order/types/ → eliminates the cycle
→ Team documents package dependency diagram: each package is a box, imports are arrows → no cycles
→ New developer joins: reads package dependency diagram, understands architecture in 10 minutes
failure_modes: Utility package becomes a dumping ground — internal/util/ starts with 2 helper functions and grows to 50 unrelated functions (string utilities, date formatting, HTTP helpers, DB utilities). Every package imports util/, creating universal coupling. Fix: split util/ by domain — internal/stringutil/, internal/timeutil/, internal/httputil/, internal/db/.

Internal package exports too much — an internal/ package exports 50 types and 30 functions but only 3 are used outside the package. The exported surface creates a maintenance burden: every exported symbol is part of the API contract. Fix: make everything unexported by default; only export what is needed by other packages.

Vendored package boundary mismatch — the team copies a third-party library into internal/vendor/ and modifies it. The modified version has different behavior than the original, causing subtle bugs when team members assume standard behavior. Fix: fork the library into a separate repo with documentation of the changes.
hidden_magic_checks: Learner must identify which package boundary is wrong given a circular import error trace (e.g., package a imports b imports c imports a) and propose the correct extraction (extract shared types, merge packages, or move the import to a lower-level package).
Learner must evaluate a given package's exported surface (15 exported types, 40 exported functions) and identify which symbols should be unexported, with justification for each.
Learner must explain why a package named internal/helpers/ is an architecture smell — the name implies no cohesion, which means the package will grow without limit and create universal coupling.
zero_magic.how_go_uses_it: Go packages are the fundamental unit of code organization. A package is a directory with Go files sharing the same package declaration. Exported names (starting with capital letter) form the public API. Unexported names are accessible within the package only. The go tool enforces acyclic imports: if package A imports B and B imports A, compilation fails. This constraint is deliberate — it forces packages to form a DAG (directed acyclic graph), which is the foundation of maintainable architecture. The internal/ convention (introduced in Go 1.4) restricts imports: packages under internal/ can only be imported by code rooted at the internal/ parent. This enforces module boundaries in mono-repos.
zero_magic.mental_model: A package boundary is a contract wall. Inside the wall, code can access everything (exported and unexported). Outside the wall, only the officially exported doorways (exported functions, types, constants) are accessible. The wall has a cost: every time a developer needs to cross it, they must use the official doorway. The benefit: the code inside the wall can be refactored, renamed, or rewritten as long as the doorways stay the same. A good package boundary is one where the cost of crossing is justified by the freedom it gives the code inside.
performance_implications: Package import overhead is paid at compile time only — importing a package adds ~1ms to compilation per 1000 packages. Runtime performance is unaffected.
Interface boundary crossing (calling a method through an interface) costs ~1ns per call. For a typical handler calling a service calling a repository, the total cost is ~3ns — negligible.
Type assertion at package boundaries (casting interface{} to concrete type) costs ~1ns. Using interface{} in exported APIs is discouraged not for performance but for type safety.
zero_magic.problem_solved: New Go developers either throw everything into one main package or create 50 tiny packages with no cohesion. Both approaches make the codebase impossible to navigate at scale. This lesson teaches the sweet spot: packages should be cohesive (all contents relate to a single domain) and have a small exported surface (the minimum needed by other packages). The learner practices identifying good vs. bad package boundaries and refactoring packages with wrong boundaries.
zero_magic.proof_of_understanding: The learner is given a Go project with 5 packages and circular import errors. They must: (1) draw the package dependency graph, (2) identify the cycle, (3) propose a fix (extract shared types, merge packages, or split the interface), (4) implement the fix, and (5) verify that all imports are acyclic. They must also document the package boundaries with a short comment explaining each package's responsibility.
zero_magic.real_world_usage: Package boundaries are the most important architectural decision in Go projects. Kubernetes has 300+ packages organized by domain (pkg/api/, pkg/kubelet/, pkg/scheduler/). Docker organizes by component (daemon/, builder/, cli/). CockroachDB organizes by SQL layer (sql/, sql/parser/, sql/exec/). Every major Go project uses packages as the primary architecture primitive. The pattern is consistent: one domain per package, small exported surface, acyclic imports enforced by the compiler.
step_by_step_execution: Identify the domain boundaries in your project: user management, billing, orders, notifications
Create one package per domain: internal/user/, internal/billing/, internal/orders/, internal/notify/
Move all types, functions, and constants related to each domain into its package
Export only what other packages need: functions, types, and constants that are called from outside the package
Run go build — if it succeeds, imports are acyclic. If it fails with import cycle, restructure to eliminate the cycle
Document the package dependency diagram in the project README — each package as a box, imports as arrows
Add an internal/ package for code that should not be imported from outside the project root
zero_magic.under_the_hood: Go's import resolution works as follows: the compiler resolves each import path to a directory, reads all .go files in that directory with the same package declaration, and builds a symbol table of exported names. Import cycles are detected during dependency graph construction: the compiler walks the import graph depth-first, marking each package as 'visiting.' If it encounters a package that is already 'visiting,' it reports an import cycle and stops. This check runs once per build and is the fastest possible cycle detection (O(V+E) where V is packages and E is imports). The internal/ convention is enforced by go/build: during import resolution, the tool checks whether the importing package's root is an ancestor of the internal/ package's directory. If not, the import is rejected with a compile error.
zero_magic.why_it_exists: Package boundaries exist because code without boundaries becomes a Ball of Mud. When every file can access every symbol, there is no encapsulation, no API surface, and no refactoring safety. A developer cannot tell whether renaming a function will break 1 file or 50. Package boundaries create intentional contracts: the exported API is the 'yes, you may use this' surface; everything else is 'internal, may change without notice.' Without package boundaries, large codebases become unmaintainable because the cost of understanding any single change requires reading the entire codebase.

items.title: Service layer

verification.expected_output: Learner can demonstrate the concept and explain it.

beginner_mistakes: Putting business logic in HTTP handlers — the handler parses the request, calls the database, formats the response, and handles errors. When the same logic is needed for a gRPC endpoint or a background job, the handler code cannot be reused. Business logic must live in the service layer, not the transport layer.

Making the service layer a thin pass-through — the handler calls service.CreateUser which calls repo.InsertUser with no transformation, validation, or business logic. The service layer adds complexity without value. A service layer must justify its existence by containing business rules, not just forwarding calls.

Letting services become god objects — internal/service/user.go has 3000 lines with 50 methods covering user CRUD, billing, notifications, and reporting. The service layer should be split by bounded context, not by entity. User billing is a different service than user profile management.
execution_timeline: Handler calls service.CreateUser(ctx, req) — the handler only parses HTTP, delegates to service
→ Service.CreateUser validates business rules: email is unique, password meets strength requirements, user is not on blocklist
→ Service calls repo.InsertUser(ctx, user) — the service abstracts the storage implementation
→ Repo returns created user — the handler formats the HTTP response with the user data
→ A new requirement: send welcome email after user creation
→ Developer adds service.SendWelcomeEmail(ctx, user) call in CreateUser — one line change in the service layer
→ The handler is unchanged — it still just calls service.CreateUser and formats the response
→ A second consumer arrives: an admin bulk-import endpoint that creates 1000 users from a CSV file
→ Admin handler calls service.CreateUser in a loop — the same business logic, no code duplication
→ The service layer proves its value: business logic is written once, used by every transport
failure_modes: Service layer depends on transport types — service.CreateUser takes http.Request as a parameter. Now the same service cannot be called from a gRPC handler or a CLI command. Fix: service methods must take only domain types (context, structs, primitives). Transport-specific types (http.Request, proto.Message) must be converted in the handler.

Service layer leaks database concerns — CreateUser returns *sql.Rows or raw database errors. The caller must understand SQL to use the service. Fix: the service layer returns domain types and domain errors. Database errors are mapped to domain errors (ErrNotFound, ErrConflict, ErrInternal) inside the repository.

Service layer has no transaction boundary — CreateUser inserts a user AND sends a welcome email, but if the email fails, the user is already inserted. The operation is not atomic. Fix: the service layer should own the transaction boundary — begin a transaction, call repositories, commit or rollback.
hidden_magic_checks: Learner must identify which code belongs in the handler vs. the service layer given a function that parses HTTP parameters, validates business rules, calls the database, and formats the response — the HTTP parsing and response formatting belong in the handler; validation and database calls belong in the service.

Learner must refactor a god-object service (50 methods across 3 domains) into separate services by bounded context — extracting UserService, BillingService, and NotificationService from a single UserService.

Learner must explain why an interface defined in the service package (type UserRepository interface { ... }) is better than importing the concrete repository type — the interface in the consumer package is the 'need to know' contract; the concrete implementation can be swapped without changing the consumer.
zero_magic.how_go_uses_it: The service layer in Go is a package (e.g., internal/service/) that contains business logic methods. Each method takes a context.Context and domain types, performs business rules, coordinates calls to repositories/external services, and returns domain types or domain errors. The service layer does NOT import HTTP or gRPC packages. It defines its own interfaces for dependencies (e.g., UserRepository interface with Insert, GetByID, Update methods). This interface-in-the-consumer pattern is idiomatic Go: the service defines what it needs, and the concrete implementation satisfies the interface.
zero_magic.mental_model: The service layer is the brain of the application. The handler is the mouth (talks to the outside world). The repository is the hands (talks to the database). The brain decides what to do (business rules), the mouth receives input and delivers output, and the hands execute the storage. The brain should not do the hands' job (SQL queries) or the mouth's job (HTTP parsing). The brain should be testable without the mouth or hands — inject mock dependencies and test the business logic in isolation.
performance_implications: Service layer interface dispatch costs ~1ns per method call — negligible for business logic. If a hot path calls a service method 100K times/second, the overhead is 100µs — still negligible.

Service method allocations (creating result structs, error wrapping) are the main cost, not the layer itself. A service method that allocates 5 intermediate values costs ~200ns in GC overhead. This is acceptable for most services but matters for latency-critical paths (<1ms).
Dependency injection in the service layer (passing interfaces in constructor) costs one allocation per service instance at startup — negligible.
Service methods that create transactions add ~100µs per transaction (db.Begin overhead) — use batch operations within a single transaction instead of per-row transactions.
zero_magic.problem_solved: New Go developers put all logic in HTTP handlers because it is the easiest place to start. When a second consumer (gRPC, CLI, background job) needs the same logic, they copy the code — creating a maintenance nightmare. The service layer centralizes business logic in one place, making it reusable across all transport layers and testable without HTTP or database dependencies.
zero_magic.proof_of_understanding: The learner is given a Go HTTP handler with 200 lines of inline business logic (validation, business rules, database calls, email sending). They must: (1) extract the business logic into a service layer, (2) define interfaces for dependencies (repository, email sender), (3) write unit tests for the service with mock dependencies, (4) verify the handler still works end-to-end with the refactored code.
zero_magic.real_world_usage: The service layer pattern is universal in production Go services. Stripe's API handlers call the service layer for every operation. Kubernetes' API server has a service layer between the HTTP handler and the storage backend. Docker's engine API uses a service layer for image and container operations. The pattern is: handler → service → repository (or external API). The service layer is the only layer that contains business logic — handlers and repositories are mechanical.
step_by_step_execution: Identify business logic in the HTTP handler: validation, business rules, calculations, error handling
Create a service package: internal/service/
Define service interface: type UserService interface { CreateUser(ctx, req) error }
Implement service: type userService struct { repo UserRepository } with business logic methods
Define repository interface in the service package: type UserRepository interface { Insert(ctx, user) error }
Implement repository in a separate package: internal/repo/postgres/
Wire dependencies in main.go: repo := postgres.NewUserRepo(db); svc := service.NewUserService(repo); handler := httpapi.NewUserHandler(svc)
Handler calls svc.CreateUser — no business logic in the handler
Test the service: create a mock repository and test business rules in isolation
Add a second consumer (CLI command) — same svc.CreateUser call, zero code duplication
zero_magic.under_the_hood: The service layer in Go is enabled by two language features: interfaces and package visibility. Interfaces allow the service to define its dependencies abstractly (type UserRepository interface { Insert(ctx, User) error }). The concrete type satisfaction is implicit — any type with an Insert method with the right signature satisfies the interface. Package visibility (exported/unexported) enforces the layer boundary: the service package exports only business types and interfaces; implementation details are unexported. The `internal/` directory convention prevents external consumers from importing implementation packages directly. The service layer does not depend on any specific transport or storage — it is a pure Go package that could be used in any context.
zero_magic.why_it_exists: The service layer exists because business logic is the most valuable and most fragile part of a codebase. It contains the rules that make money, prevent fraud, and ensure compliance. It should not be mixed with mechanical code (HTTP parsing, SQL queries, email formatting) that changes for different reasons and at different speeds. The service layer isolates business logic so it can be: (1) tested thoroughly, (2) reused across transports, and (3) changed without affecting other layers.

items.title: Repository pattern deep dive

verification.expected_output: Learner can demonstrate the concept and explain it.

beginner_mistakes: Defining repository interfaces in the implementation package — the postgres package exports a UserRepository interface and the service imports it. This forces the service to depend on the storage package for a type definition, creating a dependency in the wrong direction. The interface must be defined in the package that NEEDS it (the service), not the package that IMPLEMENTS it (the repository).

Making repository methods that mirror SQL exactly — FindByID, FindByName, FindByEmail, FindByStatus creates one method per query. When a new query is needed (FindByRoleAndStatus), a new method must be added. Fix: use a query specification pattern — FindUsers(ctx, spec UserQuerySpec) where spec contains the filter criteria. This reduces the interface surface and supports any combination of filters.

Leaking database types through the repository interface — GetUser returns *sql.Row or the repository accepts *sql.DB in its constructor. The service layer must understand database types to use the repository. Fix: the repository interface should accept and return only domain types. The *sql.DB connection is injected at the concrete implementation level.
execution_timeline: Service needs a user: calls repo.FindByID(ctx, userID)
→ Repository method constructs SQL: SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1
→ Repository executes the query: db.QueryRowContext(ctx, query, userID)
→ Repository scans the result: row.Scan(&user.ID, &user.Name, &user.Email)
→ Repository maps the DB row to a domain type: User{ID: id, Name: name, Email: email}
→ Repository returns the domain type: return user, nil
→ Service calls repo.FindByID and gets back a domain.User — no SQL types, no DB concepts
→ Test: create a mock UserRepository that returns a User directly — tests run in milliseconds with no database
→ Production: inject a *sql.DB-backed UserRepository — same service code, real database
→ Migration: switch from Postgres to MySQL — implement a new MySQLUserRepository satisfying the same interface, inject it in main.go, no service code changes
failure_modes: Repository maps to DTOs instead of domain types — GetUser returns an internal/db.UserDTO with string pointers for nullable columns. The service must convert DTO to domain User. This adds conversion code in every service method and leaks DB schema decisions into business logic. Fix: the repository should map to domain types directly — handle NULL mapping inside the repository.

Repository methods return pointers vs. values inconsistently — GetUser returns *User (nil on not found), ListUsers returns []User (empty slice on no results). The service must handle both patterns. Fix: establish a convention — single entity methods return (User, error) with ErrNotFound for missing, collection methods return ([]User, error) with empty slice for no results.

Repository implements generic CRUD for every entity — CreateUser, GetUser, UpdateUser, DeleteUser for every type. For 20 entities, that is 80 methods with identical structure. Fix: only implement the query methods the application actually uses. YAGNI (You Ain't Gonna Need It) applies to repositories too.
hidden_magic_checks: Learner must identify the dependency direction error given a diagram where the service imports the repository interface from the infra package — the interface should be in the service (consumer) package, not the repository (implementer) package.
Learner must refactor a repository that returns *sql.Rows (a database-specific type) to return domain types instead, keeping the scan logic inside the repository.

Learner must explain why a repository method named FindActiveUsersByRoleAndLastLoginDate(ctx, role string, since time.Time) is a design smell — it combines two concerns (filter by role AND filter by date) into a single method name, signaling that a query specification pattern would be better.
zero_magic.how_go_uses_it: The repository pattern in Go follows 'interface in the consumer' idiom: the service package defines type UserRepository interface { FindByID(ctx, id) (User, error) }, and the concrete implementation in a separate package (internal/repo/postgres/) satisfies the interface without importing it — the service injects the concrete type. The repository handles all SQL concerns: connection management, query construction, result scanning, error mapping (e.g., sql.ErrNoRows → ErrNotFound). The service only knows about domain types and domain errors. This enables unit testing of the service with mock repositories that return domain types directly.
zero_magic.mental_model: The repository is a translation layer between two worlds: the domain world (User, Order, Product) and the database world (rows, columns, SQL, connections). The service lives in the domain world and speaks only domain language. The repository lives in both worlds: it receives domain types, translates them to SQL, executes queries, and translates the results back to domain types. The service should never see a *sql.Row, never write a WHERE clause, and never manage a connection pool. If the database changes from Postgres to MySQL, only the repository changes — the service is isolated.
performance_implications: Repository method call overhead: interface dispatch + function call = ~2ns per method. At 1000 repository calls per request, this is 2µs — negligible.

SQL query execution (the actual database call) dominates latency — a single SELECT query takes 1-50ms depending on indexes, data size, and connection pooling. The repository's Scan + domain mapping adds 1-5µs — negligible compared to the query.

Batch operations matter: calling repo.InsertUser 1000 times in a loop creates 1000 round-trips to the database (1-50s total). Fix: implement a BatchInsert method that does one multi-value INSERT with 1000 rows (1-50ms). The repository interface should support both single and batch operations.
zero_magic.problem_solved: New Go developers embed SQL queries in HTTP handlers — SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1 right next to the response format logic. When the database schema changes, they must find and update every SQL string scattered across the codebase. The repository pattern centralizes ALL database access in one place per entity. When the schema changes, only the repository changes. When the service is tested, the repository is mocked — tests run in milliseconds without a database connection.
zero_magic.proof_of_understanding: The learner is given a Go HTTP handler with inline SQL queries and response formatting mixed together. They must: (1) extract all SQL queries into a repository package with domain type mapping, (2) define the repository interface in the service package, (3) update the handler to call the service which calls the repository, (4) write unit tests for the repository (with a real test database or a DB mock), (5) verify that no SQL string appears outside the repository package.
zero_magic.real_world_usage: The repository pattern is the standard data access pattern in Go production services. Kubernetes uses repository-like interfaces for etcd storage (pkg/registry/). CockroachDB uses a repository abstraction for its SQL layer. Standard Go ORMs like sqlx, pgx, and GORM all support the repository pattern implicitly — the ORM query builder is the repository internals, and the application wraps it in a domain-typed interface. In production Go, every database access goes through a repository layer.
step_by_step_execution: Identify all SQL queries in the codebase — grep for SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
Create a repository package per entity: internal/repo/user/, internal/repo/order/
Define repository interface in the service package: type UserRepository interface { FindByID(ctx, id) (User, error); Create(ctx, user) error; List(ctx) ([]User, error) }
Implement the interface in internal/repo/user/postgres.go: type PostgresUserRepository struct { db *sql.DB }
Map between SQL types and domain types: scan row → User struct, map sql.ErrNoRows → ErrNotFound
Inject the repository into the service: NewUserService(repo UserRepository)
Test the service with a mock repository: mockRepo returns domain types directly, no database needed
Test the repository integration: use a test database (docker or in-memory SQLite) with real queries
Verify isolation: grep -r "SELECT" internal/service/ should return nothing — no SQL in the service layer
zero_magic.under_the_hood: Go's database/sql package provides a generic SQL interface. sql.DB is a connection pool (not a single connection) — it maintains a pool of connections, manages keepalives, and retries on transient failures. The repository uses sql.DB methods: QueryContext (returns *sql.Rows), QueryRowContext (returns *sql.Row), ExecContext (returns sql.Result). Each method takes a context for cancellation and timeout. The repository's Scan method calls row.Scan, which uses reflection to map DB column types to Go types. The repository also maps DB errors to domain errors: sql.ErrNoRows → NotFoundError, pq.Error with code 23505 → ConflictError (duplicate key). This error mapping ensures the service layer never imports database-specific packages.
zero_magic.why_it_exists: The repository pattern exists because database access is a volatile dependency: schemas change, queries need optimization, connection pools need tuning, and databases get migrated. Every SQL string scattered across handlers is a maintenance liability — when the schema changes, every handler must be updated. The repository centralizes this volatility behind a stable interface. The business logic (service layer) depends on the interface, not the implementation. This is the Dependency Inversion Principle: high-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions.

items.title: Modular monolith

verification.expected_output: Learner can demonstrate the concept and explain it.

beginner_mistakes: Calling a monolith 'modular' just because it has multiple Go packages — a modular monolith requires domain-aligned packages with explicit API contracts, not just splitting code into files. If every internal package depends on each other, it is a distributed monolith, not a modular one.

Letting modules share a database schema — when modules share tables, they become coupled at the data layer. Changing the users table for the billing module breaks the notification module. A modular monolith means each module owns its data — use separate schemas or table prefixes per module.

Using in-process function calls as the only module boundary — when modules communicate through function calls with shared in-memory state, extracting a module into a separate service later requires rewriting the communication layer. A modular monolith should use explicit interfaces as the module boundary, so extracting a module means implementing the same interface over the network.
execution_timeline: Startup builds an e-commerce monolith: one main.go, one database, one deployment
→ 6 months later: 50K LOC, 5 developers, 3 domains (catalog, cart, orders) but all in one package
→ Team restructures: creates internal/catalog/, internal/cart/, internal/orders/ with explicit interfaces
→ Each module owns its database tables: catalog owns products, cart owns carts, orders owns orders
→ Module boundaries are interfaces: type OrderService interface { PlaceOrder(ctx, cart) (Order, error) }
→ Cart module holds a reference to OrderService (interface) — calls it through the interface, not directly
→ Team grows to 15 developers: 3 squads, each owns one module
→ Squad A (catalog) changes its schema — only catalog tests break, other modules are unaffected
→ Business needs: split orders into a separate service for PCI DSS compliance
→ Team extracts internal/orders/ into a separate Go service — implements OrderService over gRPC instead of in-process
→ Cart module changes one line: OrderService implementation switches from in-process to gRPC client — same interface
failure_modes: Module boundary is a Go package boundary only — modules import each other's internal types directly. When one module changes a type, all dependent modules must recompile and potentially change code. Fix: each module must have an explicit API package (e.g., internal/catalog/api/) that other modules import. Internal types stay private.

Modules share a database migration directory — a migration that adds a column to the orders table also adds an index to the products table because both are in the same migration file. Fix: each module has its own migration directory (internal/catalog/migrations/, internal/orders/migrations/) and its own migration runner.

Modules share in-memory caches — the catalog module caches product data in a global map, and the orders module reads from it. When catalog evicts the cache, orders gets stale data. Fix: each module owns its cache; cross-module data access goes through the module's API interface.
hidden_magic_checks: Learner must identify which of two module structures is a true modular monolith vs. a distributed monolith given the import graph — if every package imports every other package (dense graph), it is a distributed monolith. If imports form a DAG with clear layers, it is modular.

Learner must design the module boundary interfaces for a given business domain (e.g., a SaaS billing system with modules for subscription management, invoicing, and payment processing) — defining what each module exports and what it depends on.

Learner must explain why a modular monolith with explicit module interfaces is a better starting point than microservices for most teams — the monolith avoids network complexity, data consistency challenges, and deployment coordination while preserving the option to extract services later.
zero_magic.how_go_uses_it: A modular monolith in Go uses the internal/ package convention to enforce module boundaries. Each module is a subdirectory of internal/ (internal/catalog/, internal/cart/, internal/orders/). Each module has an exported API (internal/catalog/api/) that defines the interface other modules can use. Module implementations are unexported. Modules communicate through interfaces defined in the API package. Database access is module-scoped: each module has its own *sql.DB or *sql.Tx reference. The main.go wires modules together by creating concrete implementations and passing them as interface values to dependent modules.
zero_magic.mental_model: A modular monolith is a codebase that is structured like a set of microservices but deploys as a single binary. Each 'module' is a potential future service. The module boundary is an interface, not a network call. The difference from microservices is deployment topology (one binary vs. many), not design topology (modules with explicit interfaces).
performance_implications: In-process interface calls between modules cost ~1ns — negligible. Network calls between microservices cost 1-10ms. A modular monolith is 1000-10,000x faster for inter-module communication.

Modules sharing the same process share the same memory and CPU — one module's memory leak affects the entire application. Microservices isolate failures at the process level. The tradeoff: simpler operations (one binary, one deployment) vs. stronger failure isolation (many processes).

Test compilation for a modular monolith is faster than microservices: one go test ./... rebuilds all modules in one compilation. Microservices require building and testing each service separately with separate CI pipelines.
zero_magic.problem_solved: New Go teams either build a Big Ball of Mud monolith with no internal structure (unmaintainable at scale) or jump to microservices with 20 repos and 5 Kubernetes services (operationally overwhelming). The modular monolith is the third path: a single binary with microservice-quality internal boundaries. It gives the team the design rigor of microservices without the operational cost. When the team outgrows the monolith, extracting a module into a service is a mechanical exercise — the interface already exists.
zero_magic.proof_of_understanding: The learner is given a Go codebase with 3 domains mixed in a single package (catalog, cart, orders). They must: (1) identify which code belongs to each domain, (2) create module directories with API packages, (3) define explicit interfaces between modules, (4) ensure each module has its own database tables (separate schema or prefix), (5) verify the import graph is acyclic, (6) write a test that proves one module can be replaced with a mock implementation without affecting other modules.
zero_magic.real_world_usage: The modular monolith is the recommended starting architecture for most Go teams. Shopify (Ruby) famously ran a monolithic codebase for a decade before extracting services. GitHub's architecture started as a Ruby on Rails monolith. In Go, the modular monolith pattern is used by: HashiCorp's products (Terraform, Vault, Consul all started as modular monoliths), Sourcegraph (single binary with domain modules), and Mattermost (modular monolith with plugin architecture). The lesson: start modular, extract services only when there is a proven need.
step_by_step_execution: Identify domains: catalog (products, categories), cart (shopping sessions, items), orders (purchase history, status)
Create module directories: internal/catalog/, internal/cart/, internal/orders/
Create API packages: internal/catalog/api/catalog.go with type Service interface { ... }
Implement modules: internal/catalog/service.go implements catalog/api.Service
Separate data ownership: catalog owns product table, cart owns cart_items, orders owns orders
Wire modules in main.go: catSvc := catalog.NewService(db); ordSvc := orders.NewService(db, catSvc)
Test each module independently: mock the interfaces of dependent modules
Document module dependency diagram: catalog → (none), cart ↔ catalog (reads product data via API), orders → catalog, cart
Extract one module (optional): implement its API interface over gRPC, switch main.go to use the network implementation
zero_magic.under_the_hood: Go's internal/ convention enforces module boundaries at the compiler level. A package at internal/catalog/ can only be imported by code whose root directory is an ancestor of internal/. For a project at github.com/company/service, internal/catalog/ can be imported by github.com/company/service and its subdirectories — but NOT by any external package. This makes internal/ the ideal container for modules. Within the module, the api/ subdirectory contains the exported interface types. The service implementation is in the module root or a service/ subdirectory — unexported types that cannot be imported by other modules. Go's import cycle detection (compiler error on cycles) forces the module dependency graph to be acyclic.
zero_magic.why_it_exists: The modular monolith exists because most teams do not need microservices. Microservices solve organizational scaling problems (multiple teams deploying independently) at the cost of operational complexity (network failures, data consistency, deployment coordination). For a team of 5-15 developers, a modular monolith gives 90% of the design benefits of microservices (explicit boundaries, independent testability) with 10% of the operational cost. The modular monolith is not a compromise — it is the optimal starting point for most projects.

Can identify common mistakes.

items.title: Hexagonal architecture

verification.expected_output: Learner can demonstrate the concept and explain it.

beginner_mistakes: Creating ports for every possible adapter — defining 20 interfaces (UserReader, UserWriter, UserNotifier, UserValidator) before any adapter exists. The ports should emerge from the adapters the application actually needs, not predicted upfront. Start with one interface per adapter type (UserRepository, EmailSender, PaymentGateway) and add more as needed.

Letting the domain depend on framework types — a domain service that imports gin.Context, *sql.DB, or prometheus.Counter. The domain should be pure Go with zero framework imports. Framework dependencies belong in the adapter layer, not the domain.

Making hexagonal architecture an all-or-nothing choice — applying hexagonal architecture to every package, including utility functions and configuration reading. Hexagonal architecture is for the domain core: business logic, entities, and use cases. Configuration, CLI parsing, and logging setup are infrastructure and do not need ports and adapters.
execution_timeline: Team builds an order management system with hexagonal architecture
→ Domain core: internal/domain/order.go — type Order struct { ... } with business methods
→ Port interface: internal/domain/order.go also defines type OrderRepository interface { Save(ctx, Order) error; FindByID(ctx, OrderID) (Order, error) }
→ Inbound adapter: internal/adapters/http/order_handler.go — parses HTTP request, calls domain service, formats response
→ Outbound adapter: internal/adapters/postgres/order_repo.go — implements OrderRepository with SQL queries
→ Test: create a mock OrderRepository in the test package — tests the domain service without a database
→ New requirement: add a gRPC endpoint for order creation
→ Team adds: internal/adapters/grpc/order_server.go — implements gRPC service, calls same domain service
→ No domain changes: the domain does not know about HTTP or gRPC — it only knows about ports (interfaces)
→ New infrastructure: switch from Postgres to MongoDB
→ Team adds: internal/adapters/mongodb/order_repo.go — implements same OrderRepository interface with MongoDB driver
→ One-line change in main.go: switch from postgres.NewOrderRepo to mongodb.NewOrderRepo — domain unchanged
failure_modes: Port interface defined in adapter package — the OrderRepository interface is in internal/adapters/postgres/ and the domain imports it. This creates a dependency from domain → infrastructure, violating the Dependency Inversion Principle. Fix: the port interface must be defined in the domain package; the adapter imports the domain and implements the interface.

Adapters leak infrastructure concerns into domain errors — the postgres adapter returns sql.ErrNoRows which the domain must import to handle. Fix: the adapter must map infrastructure errors to domain errors (NotFoundError, ConflictError, InternalError) defined in the domain package.

Too many layers in the adapter — an HTTP handler goes through: adapter/http/handler → adapter/http/middleware → adapter/http/request → adapter/http/response → service. Each layer adds indirection without value. Fix: keep adapters thin — the handler should parse the request, call the domain service, and format the response. No business logic in the adapter.
hidden_magic_checks: Learner must identify the dependency direction violation given a diagram: domain imports infra/postgres for the OrderRepository interface — the interface must be in the domain package, not the infra package.

Learner must refactor a codebase that has business logic in HTTP handlers by extracting the domain, creating port interfaces, implementing adapters, and verifying no domain code imports infrastructure packages.
Learner must explain why swapping a Postgres adapter for a MongoDB adapter requires changing main.go but not the domain — the domain depends on the interface, not the implementation.
zero_magic.how_go_uses_it: Hexagonal architecture in Go follows the Dependency Inversion Principle: domain/entity packages define port interfaces (interfaces that represent what the domain needs from the outside world). Adapter packages implement those interfaces. The domain never imports an adapter package — it only imports its own types and standard library types. The wiring happens in main.go, which imports both domain and adapter packages and passes concrete adapters to domain constructors. Go's implicit interface satisfaction (duck typing) makes this pattern ergonomic: the adapter does not need to import the interface — it just needs to have methods with matching signatures.
zero_magic.mental_model: Hexagonal architecture is a power outlet. The domain is the device (lamp, phone charger). The port is the outlet shape (Type A, Type C). The adapter is the plug that connects the device to the outlet. The device does not know what power source is behind the outlet (grid, generator, battery). The outlet does not know what device is plugged in. The adapter translates between the device's needs and the source's capabilities. In Go: the domain defines the outlet (interface). The adapter (Postgres repo, HTTP handler) implements the outlet shape. main.go is the electrician that wires them together.
performance_implications: Interface dispatch through hexagonal ports costs ~1ns per call — the same as any Go interface call. No runtime overhead from the pattern itself.
Adapter-level marshaling/unmarshaling (JSON ↔ domain types, SQL rows ↔ domain types) adds 1-10µs per operation. This is the cost of the adapter translating between infrastructure and domain formats.
The main cost of hexagonal architecture is cognitive: developers must navigate more packages and understand the port-adapter distinction. This is paid once during development, not at runtime.
zero_magic.problem_solved: New Go applications tie business logic directly to specific infrastructure — an HTTP handler that writes to Postgres and sends emails via SendGrid. Changing the database or email provider requires rewriting handlers. Hexagonal architecture separates business logic (domain) from infrastructure (adapters). The domain defines what it needs (ports). Adapters implement those ports. Changing infrastructure means writing a new adapter and changing one line in main.go — the domain is untouched.
zero_magic.proof_of_understanding: The learner is given a Go service with business logic mixed in HTTP handlers and direct Postgres calls. They must: (1) extract domain types and business logic into an internal/domain package, (2) define port interfaces in the domain package, (3) implement adapters for HTTP (inbound) and Postgres (outbound), (4) wire everything in main.go, (5) write a test that mocks the outbound adapter and tests domain logic without any infrastructure.
zero_magic.real_world_usage: Hexagonal architecture is the standard pattern for Go services that need to outlive their initial infrastructure choices. Uber's Go monorepo uses hexagonal architecture for critical payment and pricing services. Monzo's Go backend uses ports and adapters for banking core services. Kubernetes' controller-runtime library follows the hexagonal pattern: controllers define ports (reconcile interfaces), and adapters implement them for different infrastructure backends.
step_by_step_execution: Identify the domain core: business entities (Order, User, Product) and business rules (canCancelOrder, calculateTax)
Create internal/domain/ package with domain types, port interfaces, and service methods
Define port interfaces in the domain: type OrderRepository interface { Save(ctx, Order) error }; type PaymentGateway interface { Charge(ctx, Payment) error }
Create inbound adapters: internal/adapters/http/ — handler parses HTTP, calls domain service, formats response
Create outbound adapters: internal/adapters/postgres/ — implements OrderRepository with SQL
Wire in main.go: repo := postgres.NewOrderRepo(db); svc := domain.NewOrderService(repo); handler := http.NewOrderHandler(svc)
Verify: grep -r "import.*adapters" internal/domain/ should return nothing — domain has no adapter imports
Test: inject a mock OrderRepository into domain service — tests run in milliseconds, no database needed
Swap infrastructure: implement MongoDB adapter, change one import in main.go — domain unchanged
zero_magic.under_the_hood: Go's implicit interface satisfaction is what makes hexagonal architecture possible without annotations or code generation. An adapter type satisfies a domain port interface simply by having methods with the right names and signatures. The compiler checks this at the point of assignment: var repo domain.OrderRepository = postgres.NewOrderRepo(db) — if postgres.OrderRepo does not have the right methods, the assignment fails to compile. This is a compile-time check with zero runtime cost. The adapter package imports the domain package (to access the interface and domain types), but the domain package never imports the adapter package. This creates the desired dependency direction: infrastructure depends on domain, not the other way around.
zero_magic.why_it_exists: Hexagonal architecture exists because infrastructure is volatile and business logic is stable. Database schemas change, cloud providers are swapped, and message queues are replaced — but the business rules (an order can only be canceled if it has not shipped) stay the same for years. Hexagonal architecture ensures that volatile infrastructure changes do not disturb stable business logic. When the team switches from Postgres to CockroachDB, they write a new adapter — the domain code is already correct and tested. Without hexagonal architecture, infrastructure changes require rewriting business logic, which introduces bugs in the most valuable part of the codebase.

items.title: Domain modeling

verification.expected_output: Learner can demonstrate the concept and explain it.

beginner_mistakes: Making domain types anemic — a User struct with only fields and getters/setters. All business logic lives in services. This is not domain modeling — it is data structures with no behavior. Domain types should encapsulate business rules: user.Cancel() should enforce that the user cannot be canceled after 30 days.

Using primitive obsession — representing OrderStatus as a string, Money as a float64, UserID as an int. The compiler cannot catch type errors: passing an OrderID where a UserID is expected compiles fine. Fix: use value types: type OrderID string, type Money struct { amount Decimal; currency Currency }.

Modeling the database schema instead of the domain — the User struct has CreatedAt, UpdatedAt, DeletedAt timestamps because the DB table has them, but the domain does not need them. The User domain type should only have fields that the business logic needs. Database concerns (timestamps, version numbers) belong in the repository mapping.
execution_timeline: Team models an Order in an e-commerce system
→ Naive approach: type Order struct { ID string; Status string; Total float64; Items []Item; CreatedAt time.Time }
→ Problem: status is a string — typo 'shipped' vs 'shipped' is a runtime bug. Total is float64 — floating point precision errors for money
→ Refactored: type OrderStatus string with const (OrderPending OrderStatus = "pending"; OrderShipped OrderStatus = "shipped")
→ Refactored: type Money struct { Amount int64; Currency string } — stored as cents, no floating point
→ Business rule: an order can only be canceled if status is pending and created less than 1 hour ago
→ Domain method on Order: func (o *Order) CanCancel() bool { return o.Status == OrderPending && time.Since(o.CreatedAt) < 1*time.Hour }
→ Domain method: func (o *Order) Cancel() error { if !o.CanCancel() { return ErrOrderCannotBeCanceled }; o.Status = OrderCanceled; return nil }
→ The Cancel method enforces the business rule — no service code can accidentally cancel an order that should not be canceled
→ Test: order.Cancel() after 61 minutes returns ErrOrderCannotBeCanceled — the rule is tested on the domain type itself
failure_modes: Domain types use interface{} or any for fields — type Order struct { Metadata any } lets any value be stored. The service must type-assert at runtime to use Metadata. Fix: use specific types. If the metadata structure varies, use a type-safe interface: type Metadata interface { Validate() error }.

Domain types are mutable everywhere — Order fields are public and can be modified from any package. A service accidentally sets order.Status = "shipped" on an order that is still pending. Fix: make fields unexported and provide behavior methods: order.Ship() can validate that the order is paid before shipping.

Over-aggressive modeling — every concept becomes a value type: Address, PhoneNumber, EmailAddress, PostalCode, CreditCard, ExpirationDate, CVV. The codebase has 50 value types and the developer spends more time converting between types than writing business logic. Fix: use value types only for concepts that have validation rules or behavior. Simple wrappers (type Name string) add ceremony without value.
hidden_magic_checks: Learner must identify which of two modelings is better for a given domain (e.g., a medical records system vs. a blog CMS) — medical records need strong type safety (type DiagnosisCode string with validation), blog CMS can use primitive types (tags []string).

Learner must refactor a primitive-typed model (string status, float64 price, int userID) into a domain-modeled version with value types and behavior methods, and verify that invalid states become unrepresentable.
Learner must explain why a domain type with public fields and no methods is a code smell — it means the business logic is elsewhere, making it harder to enforce invariants and harder to test.
zero_magic.how_go_uses_it: Go domain modeling uses concrete types with behavior methods. A domain type (Order) has unexported fields and exported methods that encapsulate business rules. Value types (Money, OrderID, OrderStatus) are defined as distinct types from their underlying primitives to prevent accidental mixing. Interfaces are used for domain capabilities (type InvoiceGenerator interface { Generate(Order) Invoice }). The domain package has zero imports from outside the standard library — it depends only on types it defines and standard library types (time, error, context).
zero_magic.mental_model: Domain modeling is making illegal states unrepresentable. If an Order cannot have a Shipped status without a ShipDate, then the Order type should not have a Status field and a ShipDate field independently. Instead, the Order should have a union-like structure: type Order struct { Pending *PendingOrder; Shipped *ShippedOrder }. Or simpler: provide methods that enforce the invariant: order.Ship(now) sets both Status and ShipDate atomically. The goal is that no valid Go program can create an invalid domain state.
performance_implications: Value types (type OrderID string) have zero runtime cost — they are the same size as the underlying type. Method calls on value types through interfaces cost ~1ns dispatch.
Domain method calls (order.Cancel(), order.Ship()) cost one function call per method — negligible. The business logic inside the method (date comparisons, status checks) dominates.

Validation on construction (NewOrder validates all fields) costs one pass over the fields — a few microseconds. This is a one-time cost per entity creation and prevents invalid entities from existing in the system.
zero_magic.problem_solved: New Go developers model the database, not the domain. Their types mirror SQL tables: User, Order, Product are structs with all fields exported, no methods, and no validation. Business rules are scattered across handlers and services. When a rule changes (orders can only be canceled within 1 hour instead of 24 hours), the developer must find every place that checks this rule. Domain modeling puts the rules ON the types: order.Cancel() checks the rule in one place. When the rule changes, only the domain type changes.
zero_magic.proof_of_understanding: The learner is given a Go codebase with anemic domain types (User, Order, Product with only fields, all exported) and business rules scattered across HTTP handlers. They must: (1) identify all business rules (e.g., order total must be positive, user email must be unique, product price cannot be negative), (2) move the rules onto domain types as methods, (3) add value types for domain primitives (OrderID, Money, EmailAddress with validation), (4) verify that invalid states are unrepresentable or guarded by construction, (5) demonstrate that the refactored domain has zero imports from outside the standard library.
zero_magic.real_world_usage: Domain modeling in Go is used by projects where business rules are complex and change frequently. Kubernetes models its API resources as domain types with validation methods (Validate(), Mutate()) on the types themselves. Docker's engine models images, containers, and volumes with domain methods for lifecycle operations. Monzo's banking core models accounts, transactions, and payments with strong domain types that prevent invalid financial states. The pattern: when the business logic is complex, put it on the types.
step_by_step_execution: Identify the core domain concepts: Order, User, Product, Payment
Define value types for primitives: type OrderID string, type Money struct { cents int64; currency string }, type Email string with validation
Define domain structs with unexported fields: type Order struct { id OrderID; status OrderStatus; total Money; createdAt time.Time }
Add constructors: func NewOrder(id OrderID, total Money) (*Order, error) — validates inputs, returns error for invalid state
Add behavior methods: func (o *Order) Cancel() error — enforces business rules, returns error if cancel is not allowed
Remove public field access — all state changes go through methods that enforce invariants
Test the domain: create orders in various states, call methods, verify that rules are enforced — tests are pure Go, no database or network needed
Verify: cross-reference the business requirements document — every rule should have a corresponding domain method or constructor validation
zero_magic.under_the_hood: Go's type system supports domain modeling through: (1) type definitions (type OrderID string) that create distinct types with no implicit conversions; (2) method declarations on any named type; (3) unexported fields that prevent external mutation; (4) constructor functions (NewOrder) that validate invariants at creation time; (5) error return values that make invalid operations explicit. Go does not have algebraic data types (Rust's enum, Haskell's sum types), so domain modelers use the 'validate on construction' pattern: accept all inputs in a constructor, validate business rules, return error if invalid, and return a valid entity if all rules pass. Once constructed, the entity's methods maintain the invariant.
zero_magic.why_it_exists: Domain modeling exists because primitive types (string, int, float64) are too permissive. An Email string can be 'not-an-email'. An OrderStatus string can be 'SHIPPEDD'. A Money float64 can have $0.1 rounding error. Domain types restrict what values are possible: type Email string with NewEmail() validation ensures only valid emails exist. type OrderStatus string with defined constants ensures only valid statuses exist. type Money struct with int64 cents ensures no floating-point errors. The goal is to use the type system to prevent bugs at compile time instead of catching them at runtime.

items.title: Invariants

verification.expected_output: Learner can demonstrate the concept and explain it.

beginner_mistakes: Assuming the database enforces all invariants — application-level invariants (e.g., 'order total equals sum of line items') are not expressible as database constraints and must be checked in code.
Only checking invariants at write time, never at read time — a data migration, backfill, or manual DB edit can create invariant violations that are invisible until the data is read months later.
Checking invariants in the wrong layer — validation in the handler passes, but the service layer has a different code path that bypasses validation, creating inconsistent state.

Concurrent invariant violation — two goroutines read the same balance (both see $100), both approve a $90 withdrawal, and both write $10 — the invariant 'balance >= 0' is violated because the second write was based on stale data.
Using panic for invariant violations in library code — an invariant check in a library panics the entire program instead of returning an error, making recovery impossible.
execution_timeline: User sends POST /withdraw with amount $90 and account ID 42
→ Handler calls service.Withdraw(42, 90)
→ Service reads account 42 from DB: balance = $100 (READ COMMITTED snapshot at time T1)
→ Service checks invariant: balance (100) >= amount (90) → true, proceed
→ Service computes new balance: 100 - 90 = 10
→ Service writes UPDATE accounts SET balance=10 WHERE id=42 — this holds a row-level lock on account 42
→ Service commits transaction — writes are visible to other transactions, lock is released
→ Concurrent withdrawal: another request reads account 42 at time T2 (before the first tx committed) — balance = $100 (stale read at REPEATABLE READ, or the read happened before the first commit)
→ Second tx also checks invariant: 100 >= 80 → true, computes new balance = 20
→ Second tx writes UPDATE accounts SET balance=20 WHERE id=42 — overwrites the first write! Final balance = $20, should be $10
→ Invariant violated: the account allowed $170 in withdrawals from a $100 balance
failure_modes: TOCTOU race: two goroutines read the invariant guard simultaneously, both pass, both write — the write order determines the final state, and both operations' preconditions are invalidated by the other.

Migration-invariant drift: a database migration adds a column that makes an existing invariant invalid (e.g., adding is_premium to an account without enforcing that premium accounts have a valid credit card on file) — existing rows violate the new invariant silently.
Deferred invariant check: an invariant is checked at request time but the actual write happens asynchronously — by the time the write executes, the invariant condition may no longer hold.

Cross-record invariant: the invariant 'sum of all invoice line items equals invoice total' requires reading all line items — if a line item is inserted between the read and the write, the invariant is checked against stale data.
hidden_magic_checks: Learner must identify the implicit invariant in a code sample before the lesson names it.
Learner must write a test that would catch an invariant violation before seeing the fix.
Learner must design an invariant check for a multi-row constraint (e.g., 'order total = sum(line_item_totals)') and identify the race condition in a naive implementation.
Learner must choose the correct isolation level (READ COMMITTED vs REPEATABLE READ vs SERIALIZABLE) for a given invariant and explain why the weaker levels allow violations.
zero_magic.how_go_uses_it: Go's standard library enforces invariants through its APIs: map access without initialization panics (invariant: map must be initialized before use), interface conversions check the type tag (invariant: type assertion must match), and io.Reader contracts (invariant: Read may return n > 0 with io.EOF). In Go services, invariants are enforced at the service layer (before writing to DB) and at the DB layer (CHECK constraints, unique indexes, foreign keys). Go's explicit error handling forces the developer to decide what happens when an invariant is violated — the error must be handled, not silently ignored.
zero_magic.mental_model: An invariant is a truth about your data that must always hold. It is not a goal — it is a constraint. 'Account balance >= 0' is an invariant. 'Accounts should generally have positive balances' is a goal. Invariants are enforced with checks at every write path, ideally at the database level (CHECK constraints) or at the service layer with a mutex or serialized access. Every read path should also check invariants defensively — stale data from migrations or manual edits can violate invariants silently.
performance_implications: Database-level CHECK constraints are nearly free (the DB evaluates them atomically with the write) — use them for single-row invariants.

Multi-row invariants (e.g., 'sum of line items = total') require a read before write — this adds latency and creates a window for race conditions; use SERIALIZABLE isolation or application-level locks.
In-memory invariant checks (mutex-protected) cost ~50ns per check — use for hot-path invariants that cannot be expressed in SQL.
Cross-service invariants (e.g., 'inventory.allocated <= inventory.total for every SKU') require distributed transactions or saga patterns — these are expensive and should be minimized.
zero_magic.problem_solved: New Go developers write business logic that assumes invariants are maintained by the database or by implicit convention. They do not add explicit invariant checks, and they do not consider concurrent access. The first time a race condition violates an invariant, the data is corrupted and the bug is invisible until a customer reports an impossible balance. This lesson makes invariants explicit: every write path must check preconditions atomically with the write, and every read path should defensively verify invariants.
zero_magic.proof_of_understanding: The learner must implement a bank transfer function that: (1) reads both account balances, (2) checks the invariant that the sender has sufficient funds, (3) performs the transfer in a transaction with SELECT FOR UPDATE to lock both rows, (4) verifies the invariant after the transfer. They must write a concurrent test (using goroutines and sync.WaitGroup) that proves the naive implementation (without locking) violates the invariant under concurrent access.
zero_magic.real_world_usage: Invariant enforcement is the foundation of data integrity in every production system. Financial systems enforce 'account balance >= 0' and 'sum of transactions = balance change'. E-commerce systems enforce 'inventory allocated <= inventory available' and 'order total = sum of line item totals'. Booking systems enforce 'seat is allocated to at most one booking'. Every violation of these invariants is a data corruption incident that requires manual reconciliation.
step_by_step_execution: Define invariant: balance >= 0 for account with ID 42
Write first version: read balance, check >= 0, subtract amount, write new balance — THIS IS BROKEN under concurrency
Write concurrent test: two goroutines both withdraw from account 42 — prove that both can pass the invariant check based on stale reads
Fix with SELECT FOR UPDATE: BEGIN; SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 42 FOR UPDATE; check invariant; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 90 WHERE id = 42; COMMIT;
Verify fix: run the concurrent test again — only one withdrawal succeeds, the second fails with 'insufficient funds'
Add defensive read check: on every read of account 42, verify balance >= 0 — catches data corruption from migrations or manual DB edits
zero_magic.under_the_hood: Database isolation levels control how concurrent transactions interact. READ COMMITTED (default in PostgreSQL) shows only committed data but allows non-repeatable reads — two reads in the same transaction may see different values. REPEATABLE READ prevents non-repeatable reads but allows phantom reads. SERIALIZABLE prevents all concurrency anomalies but requires retry on serialization failure. SELECT FOR UPDATE locks the selected rows, preventing concurrent writes and concurrent SELECT FOR UPDATE from other transactions. The lock is held until the transaction commits or rolls back. In Go, use db.BeginTx with a context and sql.TxOptions{Isolation: sql.LevelSerializable} for the strongest isolation, but be prepared to retry on serialization errors.
zero_magic.why_it_exists: Invariants exist because concurrent systems cannot assume exclusive access to data. Without explicit invariant enforcement, two concurrent requests can both read the same initial state, both validate their preconditions, and both write conflicting results — producing logically impossible states. Invariant checks at the database level (CHECK constraints, unique indexes, foreign keys) and at the application level (SELECT FOR UPDATE, optimistic locking, serializable transactions) are the only defense against data corruption in concurrent systems.
